title: Modi Pitches India as Trusted Partner at Bloomberg Forum in Delhi
excerpt: Citing 7.8% growth and reserves above $700 billion, the Prime Minister told global leaders in New Delhi that India's reforms are a matter of conviction and that the country grows with the world, not at its cost.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on October 13 that India's reform programme is driven by conviction, not compulsion.
  • He cited 7.8% growth in the first quarter, foreign exchange reserves above $700 billion, and a current account deficit of 0.61% as evidence of strong fundamentals.
  • Modi pointed to GST, the insolvency law, the consolidation of 29 labour laws into four codes, and the decriminalisation of minor offences as core reforms.
  • Warning that supply chains, energy, minerals, payments and technology are being weaponised, he pitched India as a trusted partner that grows with the world, not at anyone's cost.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi used his address to the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on October 13 to make a direct pitch to global business and political leaders: India is reforming fast, its economic fundamentals are strong, and it can be trusted as a partner at a time when trade and technology are being turned into instruments of pressure. His remarks were covered by Livemint and The Hindu BusinessLine.

"reforms are not a compulsion, reforms are our conviction"

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

The numbers Modi led with

Modi cited economic growth of 7.8% in the first quarter, foreign exchange reserves of more than $700 billion, and a current account deficit of 0.61%. He said India's banking system is at its strongest in many decades and that the country's sovereign ratings are being upgraded on the back of that strength. The figures were presented as the foundation for the rest of the argument — that India's confidence, as he put it, is at an unprecedented high.

The reform record

The Prime Minister listed the goods and services tax, which he said turned a complex web of taxes into a single national market, and the insolvency law as landmark changes. He said 29 labour laws have been consolidated into four labour codes and that hundreds of minor business-related offences have been decriminalised. The reform programme, he said, has not stopped, and he framed its pace as a matter of political choice rather than outside pressure.

Startups, welfare and energy

Beyond macroeconomic policy, Modi pointed to the spread of entrepreneurship and public programmes. The number of startups in India has crossed 2.5 lakh, he said, with about half based in smaller cities and towns and more than 45% having at least one woman director. He said 25 crore people have moved out of poverty in a decade, aided by direct transfers into bank accounts. On energy, he said renewable capacity has risen from about 75 gigawatts in 2014 to roughly 300 gigawatts, with solar schemes connecting households and farmers to cheaper power.

Power to empower

The speech's central theme was what Modi called "Power to Empower" — the idea that technology, data, knowledge and innovation should create opportunities for others rather than concentrate control. He said India supplies one in five generic medicines used globally and sent vaccines to more than 100 countries during the COVID-19 pandemic, presenting both as examples of Indian capacity serving a wider public good.

"We grow with the world and for the world"

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

Why the pitch matters now

Modi warned that supply chains, energy, minerals, payment systems and technology are increasingly being used as instruments of pressure, and that routes built by globalisation have in places become chokepoints. In that setting, he argued, the decisive question for countries choosing partners is trust — that supplies will continue in a crisis and that promises will be kept. For investors and governments in the audience, the message was that India wants a larger role in global supply chains and finance, and is asking to be judged on its growth rate, reserves and reform record. What happens next will depend on whether that pitch converts into investment and partnership decisions in the months after the forum.
